articles.title: For the Arakan Army, Recognition Must Be Earned
articles.full_text:
The Arakan Army’s quest for international recognition should be tied to Rohingya rights and accountability.
Recently, Human Rights Watch published a distressing investigative report, tellingly titled “Skeletons and Skulls Scattered Everywhere.” The report confirmed that the Arakan Army had massacred at least 170 Rohingya civilians, including 90 children, and likely killed or wounded hundreds more in the village of Hoyyar Siri (Htan Shauk Khan in Burmese) in the Buthidaung Township of Myanmar’s Rakhine State on May 2, 2024. 
This constitutes only a small fraction of the Arakan Army’s record of human rights violations against the Rohingyas. Since the ethnic armed organization (EAO) has wrested control of much of the Rakhine State in 2023-2024, it has expelled more than 150,000 Rohingyas into Bangladesh, committed war crimes — massacres, rape, and arson — against Rohingya civilians; subjected them to severe restrictions, extortion, and forced conscription; and even banned the use of the word “Rohingya” upon the threat of harsh penalty. In fact, Major General Twan Mrat Naing, the commander-in-chief of the Arakan Army and the Chairman of the United League of Arakan (ULA), had publicly denied the distinct identity of the Rohingyas, terming them as “Bengalis.”
Thus, while the Arakan Army is deliberately refusing to recognize the distinct identity of the Rohingyas, who constituted between 25 and 30 percent of the population of Rakhine State before the 2017 “cleansing operations,” it is seeking international recognition for its de facto control over Rakhine State. 
Using the geostrategic importance of Rakhine State as a leverage, the Arakan Army is trying to legitimize its territorial and administrative control over state by seeking recognition from external actors with political, economic, security, and strategic interests in the region, particularly China, India, Bangladesh, and the United States. Rakhine State holds substantial reserves of oil and natural gas, has strategic access to the Indian Ocean, hosts important Chinese and Indian geo-strategic projects, and often serves as a conduit or transit route for regional non-state armed actors. Using these factors as bargaining chips, the Arakan Army is trying to attain international recognition.
In international law, the issue of the recognition of a new state or a new government is highly complex. Since the Arakan Army has not yet made a formal declaration of independence, the question of the recognition of an independent Rakhine State is moot from the viewpoint of international law. Hence, the question is about the recognition of its government. So far, while the Arakan Army has not yet declared independence, it has formed its own government for Rakhine State, termed the Arakan People’s Revolutionary Government (APRG), which is essentially controlled by the ULA. Meanwhile, the Rakhine State Government, located in the capital Sittwe, is formally under the Tatmadaw-backed Myanmar Union Government. Thus, Rakhine State currently has two rival governments.
The situation on the ground is as follows: the Arakan Army controls approximately 90 percent of the territory of Rakhine State, along with the Paletwa Township of Chin State. In these territories, the APRG acts as the de facto government. The military-backed Rakhine State Government remains the de jure government of the state, but its de facto authority is currently restricted to the state capital Sittwe, the strategic port of Kyaukphyu, and parts of the Ann Township which the military controls. 
As long as the Rakhine State Government retains control of Sittwe, it is unlikely that any foreign state would grant de jure recognition to the APRG. However, a number of states, including China, India, and Bangladesh, have engaged with the Arakan Army in order to safeguard their interests in Rakhine State, and international institutions, particularly humanitarian actors, need to engage with the Arakan Army to avert a humanitarian crisis in the region. This creates the possibility that the Arakan Army may attempt to secure de facto recognition of its government from these states and institutions.
Whether Beijing, New Delhi, Dhaka, or any other capital would extend de facto recognition to the APRG is contingent upon the dynamics of their relations with the Tatmadaw-controlled Myanmar Union Government, the trajectory of the Myanmar civil war, and the perceptions of the urgency of their interests in Rakhine State. However, before granting any sort of recognition to the APRG, states and international institutions must take into account the following factors.
First, Rakhine State is still engulfed by war, and the APRG’s control over the region is not undisputed. The Myanmar Union Government is still engaged in an intense war against the Arakan Army, and Chin EAOs are opposed to continued Arakan Army control of Paletwa Township. Granting recognition to such an entity, even if only de facto, would be premature.
Second, the Arakan Army has displayed latent expansionist and confrontational tendencies in its actions toward other actors in the region. Its occupation of Paletwa Township has created fictions with Chin EAOs, while its actions toward Bangladesh, including repeated abductions of Bangladeshi citizens, extraction of ransom from the hostages, seizure of Bangladesh-bound vessels, imposition of illicit taxation on Bangladeshi traders, and killing of Bangladeshi citizens, have generated unease in the country. Unless the Arakan Army adopts a more moderate and conciliatory attitude, granting even de facto recognition to the ARPG would only embolden its reckless behavior and ultimately be counterproductive.
Finally, the Arakan Army has so far demonstrated no inclination to build a democratic, inclusive, and law-governed polity by ensuring the rights of all ethnic, racial, and religious communities in Myanmar. It has not only violated the rights of the long-suffering Rohingyas with impunity, it has blatantly denied the existence of a distinct Rohingya identity and effective dehumanized them by propagating the narrative that the Rohingya are “Bengali immigrants” to Rakhine State. Also, the Arakan Army has subjected other minorities, including the Chakmas and the Chin, to human rights violations. Under these circumstances, granting even de facto recognition to the APRG would be a mistake from both moral and pragmatic perspectives.
The international community and particularly the regional states should make any sort of recognition of the APRG contingent upon the Arakan Army’s recognition of the Rohingyas’ distinct identity, its commitment to safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable repatriation of all Rohingya refugees, its dedication to the creation of a democratic, inclusive, and law-governed polity, and its pledge to moderate its behaviour towards regional actors. This would go a long way in ensuring the stability of the region and a sustained peace in Rakhine State.

Since the ethnic armed organization (EAO) has wrested control of much of the Rakhine State in 2023-2024, it has expelled more than 150,000 Rohingyas into Bangladesh, committed war crimes — massacres, rape, and arson — against Rohingya civilians; subjected them to severe restrictions, extortion, and forced conscription; and even banned the use of the word “Rohingya” upon the threat of harsh penalty. In fact, Major General Twan Mrat Naing, the commander-in-chief of the Arakan Army and the Chairman of the United League of Arakan (ULA), had publicly denied the distinct identity of the Rohingyas, terming them as “Bengalis.”
Md. Himel Rahman is currently serving as Lecturer, Department of International Relations, Gopalganj Science and Technology University. His articles have been published on several platforms, including The Diplomat, The Interpreter, bne IntelliNews, Asia Times, South Asian Voices, The Nation, The Daily Star, Dhaka Tribune, and New Age.
articles.summary: The Arakan Army’s quest for international recognition should be tied to Rohingya rights and accountability.

articles.title: Tajikistan Denies a Clothing Ban Its Police Keep Enforcing
articles.full_text:
A rumor with one traceable source drew an official rebuttal in Dushanbe that buried its documented enforcement.
On July 29, Tajikistan’s Committee on Religion, Regulation of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies told Asia-Plus, the country’s only remaining major independent media outlet, that the country has adopted no law banning beards or the hijab, and that foreign assessments of Tajik religious freedom rest on unreliable sources. The denial followed a week of Russian-language reports announcing that Dushanbe had outlawed hijabs, beards, and Arab-style dress.
The reports seem to run back to a single post. On July 27, the Uzbek site Nuz.uz reported that Tajik authorities were tightening restrictions on clothing treated as alien to Tajik culture, singling out black hijabs. The report cited unnamed local sources. Lenta.ru, Trud, RBC, Fontanka, and outlets in Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan republished the report within a day, promoting what appears to be an enforcement campaign into a new law. 
Nezavisimaya Gazeta traced the wording back further, to identical posts from Instagram accounts presenting themselves as legal advisers that appeared a day before Nuz.uz, and found no Tajik-language coverage of the subject dated from 2026. Asia-Plus added that several outlets had credited the claim to Asia-Plus, which had published nothing of the kind.
The committee’s denial is narrowly accurate and largely beside the point. 
The law it declines to mention passed two years ago. Article 18 of the Law on the Ordering of Traditions, Celebrations, and Ceremonies, in force since June 2024, bars importing, selling, promoting, and wearing in public any clothing that does not correspond to national culture. It does not define what that means. As Asia-Plus noted when the law was first published, it attaches no penalty to that clause either; the fines of up to 100,000 somoni ($10,800) in the accompanying administrative code amendments cover weddings, funerals, and pilgrimage rituals instead.
This is where police discretion comes in. RFE/RL reported on July 26 that a trader in Bokhtar, held for three days over his beard and fined 180 somoni ($18), now sends officers a weekly photograph of his shaved face. Two other men said police shaved them by force and released them without charge. An official at a passport office in Khatlon said applicants with beards are told to shave, that each case is logged, and that the names go into monthly reports tracking men’s facial hair and women’s religious dress. In May, the women’s affairs committee in Rudaki district posted photographs from a village-by-village campaign steering women away from foreign clothing, then deleted them.
None of that required new legislation. Tajikistan has been a U.S. Country of Particular Concern on religious freedom since 2016, and USCIRF’s May country update found the 2024 law being enforced through campaigns against dress deemed foreign to national culture, including school visits in February. Police forcibly shaved some 13,000 men as far back as 2015, when no clothing law existed at all. A prohibition that names neither the specific offense nor the punishment can be applied by any officer and denied by any ministry.
The clothing rules are one piece of a much larger fight. Dushanbe banned the Islamic Revival Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) as an extremist organization in 2015, handed life sentences to its leaders or pushed them into exile, and has since jailed journalists, lawyers, and bloggers on the same charges. The framing has paid off. Sharing the region’s longest border with Afghanistan has made Tajikistan a durable recipient of Western counterterrorism and border-security money. As Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society argued, U.S. training helped build a coercive apparatus that Dushanbe then turned on its own citizens, most visibly during the 2022 crackdown in Gorno-Badakhshan. Overstating the threat buys both funding and the latitude to use it at home.

Russian media outlets have amplified each of these measures since Moscow’s post-Crocus Hall migration crackdown began, because the story is useful at home: proof for Russian audiences that the states supplying their labor migrants are policing their own Muslims – and so should Moscow.

articles.title: Transaction or Transformation? Inside the Russia-North Korea Relationship
articles.full_text:
How transactional is the massive shift in their relations and how sensitive is it to the Ukraine war?
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Ankit Panda and Katie Putz examine the status of the Russia-North Korea partnership. Since the signing of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in 2024, the two have held three strategic dialogues, the most recent in late July in Moscow. How transactional is the massive shift in their relations and how sensitive is it to the Ukraine war? And what does China — which has its own nuanced relations with North Korea and Russia — think about the growing closeness between Moscow and Pyongyang?

articles.title: Japan’s Intelligence Reform Has a Counterintelligence Problem
articles.full_text:
As the Takaichi administration strives to strengthen Japan’s intelligence capabilities, it’s important to build up counterintelligence capabilities too.
In order to deal with a worsening regional security environment, Japan is stepping up its intelligence capabilities. Since establishing the National Intelligence Council (NIC) this summer, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae acknowledged the threat caused by leaks of sensitive technology to foreign intelligence services. 
“We will continue discussions on ‘enhancing foreign intelligence collection’ and ‘strengthening the prevention of improper foreign influence’ while maintaining a balance with the people’s ‘liberty and human rights,’” she said at a recent press conference. 
As Japan continues its intelligence reforms, the government must also consider how to strengthen its counterintelligence capabilities. This will impact not only the development of a Japanese foreign intelligence service, but also Japanese aspirations to play a larger role in intelligence liaison relationships with friends and allies like the U.S. and its Five Eyes partnership. It is critical that Japanese policymakers strengthen Japan’s ability to defeat foreign espionage.
Counterintelligence is a critical part to the broader intelligence mission. According to James Olson, formerly the head of the CIA’s counterintelligence section, counterintelligence is “all the measures a nation takes to protect its citizens, secrets, and technology from foreign spies.” 
At first glance, this seems to primarily refer to the groups like Olson’s former organization at CIA or the counterintelligence section of the National Security Branch of the FBI. But counterintelligence also includes organizations like the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), which provides oversight of business acquisitions between American and foreign companies. There is also the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which investigates the suitability of a person to be granted access to classified information. Counterintelligence also includes counterespionage, which are activities used to penetrate, defeat, and manipulate foreign intelligence services. This creates an understanding of adversarial services, and create space for one’s own intelligence operations. What unites all of these activities and organizations is their ultimate objective being the defense of the state against foreign intelligence services.
Japan’s counterintelligence capabilities are minimal but like the broader intelligence community they have been getting stronger. Japan has two agencies that are broadly focused on countering foreign elements within Japan. The first is the National Police Agency (NPA), which is responsible for supervising the prefectural police forces in investigating criminal activity in Japan, including cyber crimes and terrorism. The second is the Public Security Intelligence Agency (PSIA), which also collects information on terrorist targets, which historically also included communist subversion. Together these are the main agencies responsible for protecting Japan’s domestic security.
Japan does not currently have a comprehensive anti-espionage law. The primary law that touches on counterintelligence is the Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets. Passed in December 2013, the law allows Japanese government agencies to limit access to information “which is publicly undisclosed and which is particularly required to be kept secret due to the risk of causing severe damage to Japan’s national security.” The law also says that unauthorized disclosure of covered information can result in incarceration up to ten years. 
To strengthen Japan’s counterintelligence regulations, the Takaichi administration supports passing a law requiring the registration of foreign agents in Japan. Like its counterparts in the United States, the law would strengthen Japanese counterintelligence through tracking the activities of foreign intelligence officers and agents and deter espionage through prosecution.
However, there remains important regulatory and institutional work that needs to be done in order for Japanese counterintelligence to be successful. The first is clearly establishing what kind of information is and is not covered by anti-espionage laws. Japan is an open society and generally protects the free flow of information in public. But states like China have exploited this openness and conduct significant open-source intelligence (OSINT) collection, especially against technical and scientific targets. According to scholars, China engages in a broad spectrum of collection activities, from “scanning technical literature to analyzing patents, reverse engineering product samples, and capturing conversations at scientific meetings. Nothing is overlooked.” Given the threat posed by China and OSINT collection, Japan should create a legal definition of covered information that both defends Japanese national security, but also protects civil liberties.
Although intelligence oversight is important to any state, it is especially acute in Japan. In the first half of the 20th century, the Imperial Japanese government strictly controlled the dissemination of information. This fear of political repression was instrumental to defeating postwar efforts to establish a Japanese version of the CIA. These concerns are still prevalent in Japan some seven decades on. Social Democratic Party lawmaker Fukushima Mizuho said that that the new NIC “infringes upon the right to privacy and other rights and paves the way for a surveillance society.” To address concerns about abuses by intelligence agencies, Japan should consider creating legislative committees dedicated to intelligence and provide oversight. Through legislative hearings and control over funding, a Diet Committee on Intelligence would provide public oversight of counterintelligence enforcement activities.
Finally, counterintelligence needs to be inculcated across the Japanese intelligence community. Most of the Takaichi administration’s intelligence reforms have been focused on centralizing operations in the Kantei. While this may be important to prevent stovepiping and turf battles, the counterintelligence mission cannot be siloed in one independent agency. Intelligence benefits from compartmentalization, especially through authority that enforces that need-to-know principle is necessary. It would also be easier to allow each intelligence agency to conduct its own counterespionage operations, as they have the best insights on how to manipulate their intelligence targets. While centralization has been a primary outcome of the Takaichi administration’s intelligence reforms, not all aspects of the counterintelligence mission can benefit from this perspective.
The Takaichi administration should be congratulated for its efforts to strengthen its intelligence capabilities. Counterintelligence has received less attention but is extremely important to the broader strengthening of Japanese intelligence. Its primary objective is protecting Japanese intelligence, whether it be through recruiting agents, hacking into secured systems, or old-fashioned break-ins. But counterintelligence’s offensive aspect is also important to understanding foreign adversary operations in Japan and creating space for Japan’s own intelligence operations. Japan also needs to decide how to both carry out this mission while also respecting important democratic norms protecting free speech and expression. Strengthening its counterintelligence capabilities through new legislative developments and establishing institutions will be critical if Japan hopes to achieve its goal of intelligence reform.

articles.title: Redesigning International Order for a G-Minus World
articles.full_text:
This is the age of hyper-multipolarity, where every plausible steering group is missing something essential.
Leaders pose for a photo at the 52nd G7 summit in Evian, France, June 16, 2026.
Debates about international order usually begin with the same question: who will lead next? Will the United States recover its authority? Will China mature into a responsible provider of public goods? Will some concert of major powers manage the transition?
The question is familiar and increasingly misleading. The defining condition of this century is not a clean transfer of hegemony from one state to another. It is the erosion of the possibility that any single state, or compact group of great powers, can supply order for everyone else.
We live in a G-minus world. The term does not simply mean that leadership is absent, as in a G-zero world. It means that every plausible steering group is missing something essential. Military reach, manufacturing capacity, financial credibility, technological innovation, demographic weight, regulatory authority, and political legitimacy are distributed across different actors. The United States remains pre-eminent in several domains, but it depends on production networks it does not control. China is central to global manufacturing and trade, but lacks the alliance structure and financial trust to underwrite a universal order. The European Union can set standards, but cannot by itself secure the system it regulates. India, Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and other consequential powers cannot be treated as rule-takers, yet they do not form a coherent governing coalition.
This is more than multipolarity. It is hyper-multipolarity: power fragmented not only among states, but across domains. Strength in one arena no longer converts automatically into authority in another.
The older theory of hegemonic stability assumed that a dominant state would supply public goods because it possessed both the capacity and the incentive to do so. Today, those two dimensions have separated. The cost of underwriting open markets, dispute settlement, maritime security, financial stability, and crisis response has risen, while the domestic political return has become less certain. Great powers are therefore tempted not only to withdraw from order, but to extract from it, through tariffs, sanctions, coercive finance, and the weaponization of interdependence.
The response cannot be to ask middle powers to become a substitute hegemon. They lack the resources, and a coalition assigned hegemonic burdens would reproduce the same incentive problem on a smaller base. The more promising question is different: how can institutions make cooperation the rational choice even when no actor can command the system?
Recent experience provides three useful answers.
First, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership survived the United States’ withdrawal from its predecessor. The remaining members preserved high-standard rules, brought the agreement into force, and later admitted the United Kingdom. The result is not a replacement for the global trading system. It is something more practical: a functioning arrangement that creates benefits for members and opportunity costs for outsiders.
Second, when the World Trade Organization (WTO) Appellate Body became unable to hear appeals, a group of WTO members initiated the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement. More than 60 WTO members now participate, and the mechanism has produced actual arbitration outcomes. It is an imperfect bridge, but it demonstrates that institutional function need not wait for unanimity.
Third, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) binds 15 politically diverse economies representing roughly 30 percent of global output and population. RCEP is less ambitious than the CPTPP in several areas, but that is partly the point. ASEAN’s central role and the agreement’s differentiated obligations made cooperation possible among states that would not accept a single power’s blueprint.
These cases suggest three design principles for a G-minus world.
The first is modularity. The next order will not be one grand covenant. It will be a set of independent but connectable modules: digital trade, critical minerals, carbon accounting, AI governance, dispute settlement, supply chain resilience, financial transparency, maritime safety, and public health. Each module must be useful on its own and more valuable when linked to others.
The second is differentiated participation. Institutions should abandon the fiction that every participant must assume identical obligations at the same speed. A state may be a core member in digital trade, a partial participant in supply chain cooperation, and an observer in security discussions. Graduated participation is not institutional weakness. It is how diverse states enter cooperation without surrendering all autonomy at once.
The third is visible benefit. Cooperation fails when costs are immediate and gains are abstract. Good institutional design front-loads practical value: faster customs treatment, mutual certification, shared stockpiles, access to trusted markets, lower financing costs, usable dispute resolution, and credible insurance against disruption. The institution becomes durable when governments can show that participation pays.
This also clarifies what democratic multilateralism should mean. Democracies do not have a monopoly on benefits to participation, and non-democracies offer genuine incentives to engagement: infrastructure finance, energy, market access, security assistance, and diplomatic protection. An incentive is not a bribe; it is what economists model as self-interest. The difference should lie in structure. Patron-client incentives are discretionary and asymmetric. An incentive-based democratic institution should be rules-based, reciprocal, transparent, contestable, and open to additional participants that willingly agree to abide by those rules.
The goal is not to restore liberal internationalism at its imagined peak. That order was never as universal or benign as its defenders remember. A more realistic objective is a multilateral-enough world: enough rules that disputes do not default to coercion; enough openness that smaller economies can reach scale; enough redundancy that one institution’s paralysis does not become system-wide failure; and enough predictability that governments and firms can plan.
Waiting for Washington to return to a leadership role and waiting for Beijing to become responsible are mirror versions of the same mistake: both entrust order to power. In a G-minus world, great power companionship and permission are optional. Small states and middle powers cannot replace hegemony, but they can build around its absence. The task is to stop asking who will rule the international system and instead start designing a system that states will choose to remain in.
This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026.

The response cannot be to ask middle powers to become a substitute hegemon. They lack the resources, and a coalition assigned hegemonic burdens would reproduce the same incentive problem on a smaller base. The more promising question is different: how can institutions make cooperation the rational choice even when no actor can command the system?
Recent experience provides three useful answers.
First, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership survived the United States’ withdrawal from its predecessor. The remaining members preserved high-standard rules, brought the agreement into force, and later admitted the United Kingdom. The result is not a replacement for the global trading system. It is something more practical: a functioning arrangement that creates benefits for members and opportunity costs for outsiders.
Second, when the World Trade Organization (WTO) Appellate Body became unable to hear appeals, a group of WTO members initiated the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement. More than 60 WTO members now participate, and the mechanism has produced actual arbitration outcomes. It is an imperfect bridge, but it demonstrates that institutional function need not wait for unanimity.
Third, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) binds 15 politically diverse economies representing roughly 30 percent of global output and population. RCEP is less ambitious than the CPTPP in several areas, but that is partly the point. ASEAN’s central role and the agreement’s differentiated obligations made cooperation possible among states that would not accept a single power’s blueprint.
articles.summary: This is the age of hyper-multipolarity, where every plausible steering group is missing something essential.

articles.title: Why the Bangsamoro Peace Process Still Depends on Trust
articles.full_text:
Elections set for September 14 will mark an important step forward, but the peace process will continue for long after the ballots have been counted.
The flag of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)’s first parliamentary elections, scheduled for September 14 after years of postponement, will complete one of the central political commitments under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB): the transition from an appointed government to an elected one.
This milestone, however, will not mark the end of the peace process writ large.
The appointment in mid-July of a new chair of the Philippine Government Peace Implementing Panel illustrates why the implementation of the CAB remains an ongoing political process. After months without a permanent government counterpart to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), a vacancy that had prompted the MILF to temporarily pause some peace process engagements, the appointment restored the principal bilateral mechanism responsible for implementing the CAB. More importantly, it signals that the difficult work of implementing the agreement will continue long after the ballots are counted.
Earlier this year, I argued that the elections would test the Bangsamoro peace process. That remains true, but just as important is the question of what comes after them. The remaining commitments under the CAB, including the completion of the decommissioning of combatants, the socioeconomic transformation of war camps, the dismantling of private armed groups, and transitional justice, still require sustained cooperation between the Philippine government and the MILF regardless of who wins the elections.
This challenge has become increasingly visible over recent months.
The MILF, long accustomed to operating as a relatively unified movement, has entered a period of genuine electoral competition. The United Bangsamoro Justice Party, led by many of the movement’s senior political leaders and peace negotiators, now competes against the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which draws support from several former MILF commanders alongside established regional politicians. The Commission on Elections (COMELEC)’s recognition of the two parties as the region’s dominant majority and dominant minority political parties institutionalized the electoral competition that had emerged within the MILF itself.
None of these developments represents a failure of political normalization. Peace agreements are expected to transform armed opposition into democratic competition, and political differences are inevitable. The question is whether those differences continue to be managed through democratic institutions rather than through force of arms.
This question has become more pressing as the elections approach.
COMELEC has placed several areas in the BARMM under its highest category of election concern because of longstanding security risks.  Recent localized attacks on military detachments have also prompted the Philippine government and the MILF, through the Coordinating Committee on the Cessation of Hostilities (CCCH), to jointly condemn the violence, warning that it threatens not only public safety but also the gains of the peace process.
The MILF’s decision to temporarily pause its bilateral peace process engagements with the national government did not extend to the ceasefire architecture established under the CAB.  The continued operation of peace implementing mechanisms such as the CCCH and the Ad Hoc Joint Action Group, therefore, demonstrates the MILF’s decision to preserve security cooperation with the Armed Forces of the Philippines despite growing strains in its political relationship with the national government.
Political tensions have also become more visible within Bangsamoro communities. Legal petitions on the constitutionality of the leadership and composition of the interim Bangsamoro government, parliamentary scrutiny of governance, and successive public rallies in Cotabato City framed respectively around anti-corruption and accountability and the faithful implementation of the CAB reflected concerns, both in BARMM and national arenas, about the political legitimacy of the transition.
As divisions within the MILF became more pronounced, governance and implementation of the peace agreement increasingly came to be associated with two factions of the movement: the interim Bangsamoro government, which exercised regional executive authority during the transition, and the MILF leadership, which remained the principal signatory to the peace agreement.
This emerging political divide also reshaped the narrative surrounding the  Bangsamoro transition. For some local observers, the political messaging of both the national government and the interim Bangsamoro leadership increasingly framed the transition in terms of governance reforms and the forthcoming parliamentary elections rather than the continuing implementation of the CAB. While governance and elections are indispensable, such emphasis also risked reinforcing the view that the success of the Bangsamoro project would be measured primarily by governmental performance rather than by completion of the CAB that made the BARMM possible.
It was in this political environment that perceptions of national government involvement in the BARMM assumed greater significance. The issue was not Manila’s continued engagement in regional government’s affairs, which is inherent in the asymmetrical relationship between the national government and the BARMM established under the CAB, but whether that engagement was perceived to privilege governance and the electoral process over the continuing implementation of the peace agreement.
Such a distinction obscures the nature of the Bangsamoro transition. BARMM did not emerge independently of the peace process; it is one of its principal outcomes. Good governance and faithful implementation of the CAB should reinforce one another rather than being treated as competing priorities. The challenge now is to sustain the confidence necessary for the Philippine government and the MILF to carry the peace process through and beyond the elections.
This is why the appointment of a new Government Peace Implementing Panel chair is an important development.
Beyond filling a vacant position, the appointment restores a political counterpart for engagement with the MILF at a time when implementation has become more complex and confidence between the parties has come under greater strain. Mel Senen Sarmiento, who was appointed Secretary of the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation, and Unity (OPAPRU) in April, following leadership changes in the government’s peace office amid public criticism of his predecessor, now also chairs the Government Peace Implementing Panel for the Bangsamoro peace process.  By vesting both responsibilities in a Cabinet Member, the Philippine government has linked responsibility for overseeing peace policy with its principal mechanism for engaging the MILF on implementation issues, projecting continuity and renewed political commitment to implementing the CAB.
Describing the arrangement, Sarmiento said it would provide “seamless alignment” between peace policy and implementation.  His MILF counterpart, Mohagher Iqbal, offered an equally telling response: “He is a Cabinet Member: he can commit.” Civil society peace advocates also welcomed the appointment as an important step in restoring momentum to the implementation of the CAB, while emphasizing that its significance would largely depend on whether it translated into concrete progress on the CAB’s remaining commitments. These responses demonstrate the central reality of the Bangsamoro peace process: implementation of the CAB depends not only on institutions but also on confidence that those representing each party possess both the political authority and the political will to honor the commitments they made across the negotiating table.
Beyond issues like voter turnout and the absence of election-related violence, the success of the Bangsamoro’s first parliamentary elections should be judged by whether they leave behind sufficient trust for the Philippine government and the MILF to complete what remains unfinished under the CAB.
